findings.claim: Oakland currently lists a year-round free compost distribution point at West Oakland Farm Park, 2847 Peralta Street, through Acta Non Verba. The city says it is made from food scraps and yard waste collected from Oakland homes and businesses.
findings.operational_limits: Tue–Fri 1–6 pm and Saturday 10 am–2 pm at retrieval; self-load with own containers; may run out between deliveries. No allocation or availability guarantee.

findings.claim: WM describes an Altamont facility for residential green waste co-collected with food waste; its published design capacity is up to 500 tons/day.
findings.operational_limits: Undated historical facility page. Do not equate design capacity with throughput, surplus, or the present destination of every Oakland organics stream.

findings.claim: UC IPM describes tomatoes as warm-weather plants, with an approximate May planting window for Monterey County north and December–March for desert valleys. Seed starts may precede regional planting by 4–6 weeks.
findings.operational_limits: These are approximate planting windows, not days to harvest or December output. Winter Bay Area outdoor tomatoes are not a dependable planned reserve.

findings.claim: Radishes are a cool-season crop; UC IPM lists possible year-round planting on the California coast and successive planting for continuity.
findings.operational_limits: Microclimate, pests, soil and water still control yields. This source reading did not admit a universal numeric days-to-harvest promise.

findings.claim: Compost nitrogen availability depends on decomposition, carbon-to-nitrogen ratio, soil temperature and moisture. Applying compost solely to meet nitrogen can overapply phosphorus and potassium. UC advises matching soil tests and compost nutrient analysis.
findings.operational_limits: Compost is a nutrient-recycling buffer, not unlimited or immediately plant-available fertilizer. Legume cover crops can add nitrogen with suitable biology and time; they do not create phosphorus or potassium.

findings.claim: Food support can fail through a timing gap even where annual food throughput is large: usable stock is exhausted before alternative deliveries or new harvests arrive.
findings.operational_limits: No measured Bay Area or rural Tennessee service-cover days admitted. Turnover, shelf life, accessible stock cover and replacement lead time must be recorded separately.

findings.claim: Seasonal donor networks can complement local growing if the origin has surplus after local needs, and packing, temperature control, winter roads, fuel, drivers, unloading and distribution remain usable.
findings.operational_limits: This is a route-validation framework, not proof of an operating December tomato corridor. Fresh tomatoes are only one possible crop; preserved foods and seasonal crops may bridge waiting with fewer dependencies.

candidate_actions: Use the existing free compost pickup as an immediate input lead; transport pooling can make a bulky resource accessible to people without vehicles.
Begin growing from modifiable space, clean suitable containers or tested beds, seasonal crop choices and dependable water; let the social structure develop with use.
Keep nutrient adequacy as a mass-balance and timing question: soil and compost tests, harvest exports and expected mineralization, not compost volume alone.
Assess community service reach by travel time, distribution frequency, eligibility and missed visits rather than claiming the Bay Area is sufficient or rural Tennessee uniformly deficient.
Overlap stored food, scheduled deliveries and growing crops so a crop planted after disruption is not counted as food available now.
